questions.question: What extra feature turns a linear map into a linear operator?
options: Its domain and codomain are the same space
It sends every vector to zero.
It is defined only on real numbers.
It must have exactly one eigenvalue.

questions.question: Why does repeated application make sense for a linear operator?
options: Linear operators have no codomain.
The output lies in the same space as the input, allowing reuse
Every operator sends vectors to scalars.
Repeated application is possible only for zero maps.

questions.question: What does the notation $\mathcal L(V)$ mean?
options: The list of all bases of $V$.
The kernel of every map on $V$.
$\mathcal L(V,V)$, the linear operators on $V$.
The set of all vectors in $V$ with length one.

questions.question: Which familiar map is a linear operator on every vector space $V$?
options: A map with no vector-space structure.
A map from $V$ to a different space $W$.
The identity map $I(v)=v$.
A function that sends vectors to unrelated scalars only.

questions.question: Why are eigenvalues naturally associated with linear operators?
options: They concern a map from a vector space back to itself.
They require the codomain to be a scalar field only.
They are defined for arbitrary functions between unrelated sets.
They are unrelated to square matrix representations.

questions.question: Which map is a linear operator?
options: $A:V\to W$ with $V\ne W$
$A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$
$A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$
$A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3$

questions.question: If $A\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3)$, what is the codomain of $A$?
options: $\mathbb R^3$
$\mathbb R^2$
$\mathcal L(\mathbb R^3)$
$\mathbb R$

questions.question: Which expression relies on applying an operator twice?
options: $vA$ where $v$ is only a vector
$A+v$
$A^2v=A(Av)$
$A:V\to W$ with $W\ne V$

questions.question: On the vector space of all polynomials, what does the derivative operator do to $p(x)=x^3$?
options: It sends $p$ to $3x^3$.
It is not an operator on polynomials.
It sends $p$ to $3x^2$.
It sends $p$ to $x^4/4$.

questions.question: Which square matrix can represent a linear operator on $\mathbb R^2$?
options: A $3\times2$ matrix.
A $2\times2$ matrix.
A $1\times3$ matrix.
A $2\times3$ matrix only.

questions.question: Why is a map $A:V\to W$ with $V\ne W$ not called a linear operator?
options: It does not map the space back to itself
It cannot have a domain.
It cannot be linear.
It must send every vector to zero.

questions.question: What is the difference between a linear map and a linear operator?
options: A linear map can never be represented by a matrix.
A linear map is always nonlinear unless it is square.
A linear operator is the special case $A:V\to V$.
A linear operator has no scalar multiplication rule.

questions.question: Why does matrix power correspond to the operator viewpoint?
options: Powers turn matrices into vectors.
Powers represent repeated composition of a space-to-itself map
Matrix powers ignore the domain and codomain.
Powers can be taken for every rectangular matrix.

questions.question: Let $R:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ rotate every vector by $90^\circ$. How should $R$ be classified?
options: As a linear map but not an operator.
As a scalar, not a map.
As a map from $\mathbb R^2$ to $\mathbb R^3$.
As a linear operator on $\mathbb R^2$.

questions.question: If $I(v)=v$, what is $I(I(v))$?
If $D$ is the derivative operator on polynomials, what is $D^2(x^3)$?
Can a linear operator be studied through determinants and eigenvalues, while a general map $V\to W$ usually cannot?
options: Only if the operator is the zero map.
Only if $V$ has dimension one.
No, determinants are defined for every map between vector spaces.
Yes, those notions require an operator or a square matrix representation.

questions.question: Why does the notation $A^3$ carry more information than just “three copies of $A$”?
options: It means $A$ is applied to three unrelated spaces.
It means $A$ has exactly three eigenvalues.
It means the operator is composed with itself three times.
It means the entries of every vector are cubed.

questions.question: If $A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ is represented by $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is $A(1,1)$?
Which proposed product of an operator with itself is dimensionally meaningful?
options: If $A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3$, then $A^2$ is automatically meaningful.
If $A:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$, then $A^2$ is meaningful.
No linear map can ever be composed with itself.
If $A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$, then $A^2$ maps $\mathbb R^2$ to $\mathbb R$.
